clue.text: Preserve monkeys for the table ?

parts.note: to preserve food is to can it
apes are primates, loosely monkeys

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether to bottle some monkeys and serve them up at dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a description rather than a synonym: these savoury bites are made to go on the table at a party, and the question mark admits the looseness.
explanation.definitionFit: Small savoury morsels on bread or biscuit are served at drinks parties and laid out on a buffet.

clue.text: Stick to the local firm

parts.note: Co. is the abbreviation for company, a firm
local means of this place, and 'here' is this place

explanation.surface: Someone resolves to stay loyal to the neighbourhood business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The local' looks like a British pub, but here it means 'in this place', HERE; the firm's CO goes first.
explanation.definitionFit: To stick together is to hold fast as one mass, which is the sense of the verb.

clue.text: Mistake path in New Hampshire, a flare needed

indicators.note: the shuffled letters sit within the state's abbreviation, signalled by in

parts.note: NH is the postal abbreviation for the US state of New Hampshire

indicators.note: to mistake the word path is to get its letters wrong, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A hiker has taken the wrong trail in New Hampshire and needs to signal for rescue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mistake' rearranges PATH to APHT, which 'in' puts inside NH; A follows. The definition reads as 'what a flare needs'.
explanation.definitionFit: This volatile oily fuel was burned in old flares and lamps, so it is the stuff a flare needs.

clue.text: Plan in favour of the mass unit

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of
a gramme is a unit of mass in the metric system

explanation.surface: A scheme is backed because it suits the masses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The mass' looks like the common people, but 'mass unit' is a unit of weight, the gramme.
explanation.definitionFit: A schedule of things to be done is a plan, the noun sense here.

clue.text: Top dog, say ?.

parts.note: 'top dog' usually means the winner, but read literally it is a dog named after the sky above, which is on top of everything; the breed comes from a Scottish island whose name sounds the same

explanation.surface: Someone is named as the boss of the outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: The breed is named after the Hebridean island of Skye, which sounds like 'sky', the top of everything; 'say' warns of the sound-alike.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-haired Scottish terrier breed whose island name sounds like the heavens overhead, so a dog from the top.

clue.text: Surely the right one for the dog to bark up

definitions.text: Surely the right one for the dog to bark up

parts.words: Surely the right one for the dog to bark up
parts.note: a dog that is barking up the wrong tree has made a mistake; the right tree for a dog that bays would be named after that very cry, and trees have bark

explanation.surface: A hound has finally found the correct tree to bark up.
explanation.walkthrough: Hounds bay, and a tree has bark, so a dog baying beneath a laurel of this name is barking up exactly the right tree.
explanation.definitionFit: The sweet laurel whose leaves go into cooking shares its name with the deep cry of a hound.

clue.text: Cry of 27 before the upset

parts.note: 27 across is a London district whose name splits into a young sheep plus the word 'the' turned round; take away that upset 'the' and the young sheep remains, whose cry is wanted

explanation.surface: Someone shouts at a match just before the shock result.
explanation.walkthrough: 27 across, LAMBETH, is LAMB followed by THE written backwards, so '27 before the upset' is a lamb; a lamb's cry is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The bleat of a sheep or lamb is written as this short cry.

clue.text: Many a hoodlum apparently behaves like one

definitions.text: Many a hoodlum apparently behaves like one

indicators.note: apparently signals that the answer is plainly visible within the words many a hoodlum

explanation.surface: Lots of thugs seem to act like boors.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: a hoodlum is a coarse lout, which is what the answer means.
explanation.definitionFit: Swift's brutish humans in Gulliver's Travels gave their name to any coarse, uncouth lout, the kind a hoodlum is.

clue.text: ' That will be ere the set of sun ' said the third witch

definitions.text: ' That will be ere the set of sun ' said the third witch

parts.words: ' That will be ere the set of sun ' said the third witch
parts.note: in the opening scene of Macbeth the first witch asks when the three shall meet again, and the third replies with this line: the clue describes the coming together it promises

explanation.surface: A quotation from Macbeth, with its speaker named.
explanation.walkthrough: The line answers 'When shall we three meet again?', so it fixes the time of the witches' next gathering.
explanation.definitionFit: A meeting again of people who have been apart, as the three witches plan to do.

clue.text: A singular spectacle !.

parts.note: 'singular spectacle' sounds like a remarkable sight, but read as one spectacle lens, the singular of spectacles

explanation.surface: Someone marvels at an extraordinary sight.
explanation.walkthrough: Spectacles are a pair of lenses; one on its own, a monocle, is a 'singular spectacle'.
explanation.definitionFit: A single lens worn in one eye socket, a monocle, is the one-lens version of a pair of glasses.

clue.text: Labour man took her girdle

parts.note: Labour looks like the British political party, but the man is Hercules, whose ninth labour was to take the girdle of the Amazon queen

explanation.surface: A Labour Party politician has made off with a woman's corset.
explanation.walkthrough: Hercules performed twelve labours; one was fetching the girdle of the queen of the Amazons, so she is 'her'.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth she was the Amazon queen whose belt Hercules was set to win as one of his twelve tasks.

clue.text: Establishment gets us in to dig up the weeds

indicators.note: in tells us the word us goes inside the gardening word

parts.note: to hoe is to dig up weeds with a garden tool
taken as written

explanation.surface: A firm takes us on to do some weeding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In to' reads as 'into', but 'in' is the container signal and 'to dig up the weeds' is HOE.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm or business, as in a publishing concern, is an establishment.

clue.text: Two way revolver

indicators.note: two way says the word can be read in either direction and still be the same

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: A gun that fires both ways.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolver' wants to be a pistol; it is anything that spins, and the word reads the same both ways.
explanation.definitionFit: The spinning part of a machine, such as a helicopter's blades, is something that turns round.

clue.text: What an artist was Sweeney Todd !

definitions.text: What an artist was Sweeney Todd !

parts.words: What an artist was Sweeney Todd !
parts.note: the demon barber of Fleet Street was a hairdresser, an artist of the barber's chair, so the adjective for barbers is wanted

explanation.surface: Someone admires the fictional murderous barber's talent.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'tonsorial artist' is an old jocular name for a barber, and Sweeney Todd was the murderous barber of Fleet Street in Victorian melodrama.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means relating to barbers and hairdressing, which was Todd's trade.

clue.text: None in class can be so ridiculous

indicators.note: can be says the letters of the three words could be made into something else

explanation.surface: A teacher declares nobody in the form could be that absurd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can be' rearranges NONE IN CLASS, eleven letters, into the answer; 'so' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Absurd and without sense, the meaning of ridiculous.

clue.text: Forge instruments to quarrel with

definitions.meaning: the tools a blacksmith uses at the anvil
the idiom for fighting or arguing furiously

explanation.surface: Blacksmith's tools that might be used in a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: To go at it this way is an idiom for arguing fiercely and noisily.
explanation.definitionFit: A smith's tools at the anvil, and to fight this way means to argue with great vigour.

clue.text: A four-letter word from the Greek

definitions.text: A four-letter word from the Greek

parts.words: A four-letter word from the Greek
parts.note: 'four-letter word' suggests a swear word, but it is simply a word of four letters, named with Greek roots for four and letter

explanation.surface: Someone learns a rude Greek word.
explanation.walkthrough: The Greek roots mean 'four' and 'letter'; the name is used for the four Hebrew letters of the divine name.
explanation.definitionFit: A word or name made of four letters, built from Greek elements meaning four and writing.

clue.text: Transferred as over-subscribed

indicators.note: in a down clue the first word sits over the second in the grid

parts.note: to subscribe a document is to sign it

explanation.surface: Something was moved because too many signed up for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over-subscribed' reads as one word, but 'over' places AS above SIGNED in this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To be made over to someone else, as property or rights are, is to be transferred.

clue.text: Enters with one dog, one cat -a possible example

definitions.text: Enters with one dog, one cat -a possible example

parts.words: Enters with one dog, one cat -a possible example
parts.note: this reads like an odd entrance, but it is the sort of italic instruction printed in a play script telling the actors who comes on

explanation.surface: Someone arrives accompanied by a dog and a cat.
explanation.walkthrough: Scripts print instructions like 'Enter, with a dog' or 'Exit, pursued by a bear' for the actors.
explanation.definitionFit: An instruction printed in a script for movement or action on stage, like an entrance.

clue.text: Whatever his feet are like, the churchman could have a clay toe !

indicators.note: could have suggests the letters of clay toe may be rearranged into the churchman

explanation.surface: Whatever his feet look like, a cleric might have a toe of clay.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface plays on 'feet of clay', a hidden flaw; 'could have' rearranges CLAY TOE.
explanation.definitionFit: An assistant who serves the priest at the altar is a junior churchman.

clue.text: Colourful work on a railway

indicators.note: in a down clue the first pieces sit on top of the railway word

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work
a railway is a line

explanation.surface: Engineering work is being done on a railway line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' puts OP and A above LINE in this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Showing the shifting play of hues seen in an opal, so iridescent and colourful.

clue.text: Tool hard to part with ?

definitions.meaning: a painful parting or separation, a sharp emotional pull

explanation.surface: A tool that its owner cannot bear to lend.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is the noun for a painful parting: leaving home is a real one.
explanation.definitionFit: A spanner for gripping nuts, and also a painful parting that tears at the feelings.

clue.text: Here is different writing on the weather maps

parts.note: other means different
MS is short for manuscript, a piece of writing

explanation.surface: Someone notes the strange script printed on the weather charts.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition describes the answer by where it appears: lines on weather maps; 'Here' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Lines joining places of equal temperature are drawn across weather charts.

clue.text: Keen follower of the papers

parts.note: this sounds like an avid newspaper reader, but in the game of hare and ... runners chase a trail of scattered paper

explanation.surface: Someone who reads the press avidly.
explanation.walkthrough: In a paperchase, or hare and hounds, the hares lay a trail of paper scraps and the chasers follow it.
explanation.definitionFit: A hunting dog, and the name for a chaser in a paperchase, is a keen pursuer.

clue.text: Robin's song in the commercial ?

parts.note: an ad is a commercial
an air is a song or tune

explanation.surface: Someone hears a robin's birdsong used in a television advertisement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Robin' is not the bird but the hero of the old song 'Robin Adair'; his surname is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of the Robin in the traditional Irish song, so what belongs to him.

clue.text: You get an odd liqueur here

indicators.note: odd suggests the letters of you and an are out of their usual order

explanation.surface: A bartender says you'll find a strange liqueur at this bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd' rearranges the five letters of YOU and AN.
explanation.definitionFit: A French brandy liqueur flavoured with fruit kernels, giving it an almond taste.

clue.text: Electrical flex one has on a musical instrument

parts.note: AC is alternating current, electrical
a flex is an electrical cord
I is the Roman numeral one
taken as written

explanation.surface: An electric cable is plugged into a musical instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flex' wants to be a verb; it is the British word for an electric cable.
explanation.definitionFit: A squeezebox with bellows and keys or buttons is played as a musical instrument.

clue.text: It's " in among the bearded barley."

definitions.text: It's " in among the bearded barley."

parts.words: It's " in among the bearded barley."
parts.note: the quotation is from Tennyson's Lady of Shalott, and the 'beard' of barley is made of bristles found in among the ears

explanation.surface: A line of Tennyson about reapers in a barley field.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's line is 'In among the bearded barley'; the beard of barley consists of these bristles.
explanation.definitionFit: The bristle that grows from a grain husk is what makes barley look bearded.

clue.text: Dr East's study of China

parts.note: taken as written
E for east plus the possessive S
a den is a private study

explanation.surface: A doctor named East writes an academic study of China.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' is not the country but porcelain from Meissen near this German city.
explanation.definitionFit: Fine porcelain made near this Saxon city is known by its name, as a kind of china.

clue.text: Walk to a transpontine palace

definitions.meaning: the ... Walk is a Cockney dance from a 1930s musical
transpontine means across the bridges, south of the Thames, where the Archbishop of Canterbury's London palace stands

explanation.surface: Someone strolls over the river to a palace.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'Walk' is a 1937 Cockney dance from Me and My Girl; the palace is the Archbishop of Canterbury's London home in this south London district.
explanation.definitionFit: A Cockney dance named after this London district, and the archbishop's palace across the river there.
